definition: The money moving into and out of your accounts over a period, such as a month. It is not the same as an account balance, which is the amount held at one moment.
The cash gained or lost over a set period: total cash in minus total cash out.
A plan that shows how much money is expected to come in and go out over a future period. For each period: closing balance = opening balance + expected money in - expected money out.
A way of tracking all the money coming in and how it is spent: list your income, sort your spending into categories, and compare the two.

sources.title: Create a household budget for your family (MoneyHelper)

definition: The difference between the budgeted amount and the actual amount of an income or expense line. Spending less than budgeted is favorable; spending more is unfavorable.
Matching your own record of an account's balance against the bank's statement, and examining any difference between the two.
Money set aside over a period of time for a known future expense. In personal budgeting it is a category you pay into regularly for a planned cost.
A cash reserve set aside specifically for unplanned expenses or financial emergencies.

sources.title: An essential guide to building an emergency fund (Consumer Financial Protection Bureau)

definition: A cash reserve kept on hand to offset unplanned cash outflows: the level you do not want your cash to fall below.
The amount in an account at the start of a period. The closing balance of one period is carried forward as the opening balance of the next.
The amount of money in an account at a given time.
The amount owed on a credit card at the end of a billing cycle. Paying it in full avoids interest.

sources.title: What Is the Statement Balance on a Credit Card? (Experian)

definition: Fixed expenses do not change from month to month. Variable expenses can change each month depending on your usage.

sources.title: Fixed vs Variable Expenses: What's the Difference? (Chase)

definition: The share of after-tax income that is saved: saving divided by disposable (after-tax) income.

sources.title: Measuring How Much People Save: An Inside Look at the Personal Saving Rate (U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis)
